items.stem: What are the products of the complete combustion of an alkane?
items.answer: carbon dioxide and water
items.markingKey: Excess oxygen: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O.

items.stem: Explain why the reaction of methane with chlorine is called a photochemical reaction.
items.answer: It needs ultraviolet light to provide the energy to start the reaction.

items.stem: Explain why incomplete combustion of alkanes is dangerous in homes.
items.answer: With too little oxygen, carbon monoxide forms; it is colourless, odourless and toxic.

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈.
items.answer: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of butane, C₄H₁₀.
items.answer: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O

items.stem: Mateo investigates the reactions of propane, a member of the alkane homologous series. (a) Name the toxic gas formed if the supply of air is limited, and explain why it is toxic. (b) Explain why propane does not decolourise aqueous bromine.
items.answer: (a) Carbon monoxide: it reduces the ability of the blood to carry oxygen. (b) It is saturated (no C=C bond), so it cannot undergo addition.

items.stem: What condition is needed for methane to react with chlorine?
items.answer: ultraviolet light

items.stem: Explain why a mixture of products forms when methane reacts with excess chlorine.
items.answer: More than one hydrogen can be substituted in turn: CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄ can all form.

items.stem: Explain why alkanes are used as fuels.
items.answer: Their combustion is very exothermic, releasing a lot of energy, and they burn cleanly in excess oxygen.

items.stem: Which is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of butane?
items.answer: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O

items.stem: Calculate the volume of oxygen needed to burn 20 cm³ of butane completely, and the volume of carbon dioxide formed. 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O (all volumes at r.t.p.)
items.answer: 130 cm³ O₂; 80.0 cm³ CO₂
items.markingKey: volume ratio = mole ratio [1]; O₂ = 20 × 13/2 = 130 cm³ [1]; CO₂ = 20 × 4 = 80.0 cm³ [1]

items.stem: A gas cylinder contains ethane, which is burned in a camping stove. (a) Explain why ethane does not decolourise aqueous bromine. (b) Write the equation for the reaction with chlorine to form a monochloro product.
items.answer: (a) It is saturated (no C=C bond), so it cannot undergo addition. (b) C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl

items.stem: What are the conditions for catalytic cracking?
options: room temperature and a nickel catalyst
items.answer: high temperature and a catalyst
items.markingKey: Large alkane molecules are heated (about 500 °C) over a catalyst such as aluminium oxide or silica.

items.stem: Explain why aqueous bromine can be used to distinguish between an alkane and an alkene.
items.answer: Alkenes are unsaturated and undergo addition with bromine, decolourising it (orange → colourless); alkanes are saturated and do not react, so the solution stays orange.

items.stem: Explain why cracking always produces at least one unsaturated product.
items.answer: A long alkane does not have enough hydrogen atoms for all the smaller molecules to be saturated, so at least one alkene (or H₂) forms.

items.stem: Complete and balance the equation for the cracking of C₁₂H₂₆ into C₆H₁₄ and ethene only: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₆H₁₄ + ...
items.answer: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₆H₁₄ + 3C₂H₄

items.stem: C₁₃H₂₈ is cracked to give C₁₀H₂₂ and one other product. Deduce the formula of the other product, write the equation and describe a test to show the product is unsaturated.
items.answer: C₃H₆; C₁₃H₂₈ → C₁₀H₂₂ + C₃H₆; add aqueous bromine: turns from orange to colourless.
items.markingKey: 1 mark formula; 1 mark balanced equation; 1 mark test and result [3]

items.stem: C₈H₁₈ is cracked to give C₆H₁₄ and one other product. Deduce the formula of the other product, write the equation and describe a test to show the product is unsaturated.
items.answer: C₂H₄; C₈H₁₈ → C₆H₁₄ + C₂H₄; add aqueous bromine: turns from orange to colourless.
items.markingKey: 1 mark formula; 1 mark balanced equation; 1 mark test and result [3]

items.stem: Long-chain alkanes such as C₁₁H₂₄ are in low demand, so they are cracked: C₁₁H₂₄ → C₇H₁₆ + 2C₂H₄. (a) Describe a test to show that ethene is unsaturated. (b) Name the product when ethene reacts with bromine and state the type of reaction.
items.answer: (a) Aqueous bromine turns from orange to colourless. (b) 1,2-dibromoethane; addition

items.stem: An oil refinery in Bangkok cracks C₁₀H₂₂ to make petrol and propene. (a) Explain why cracking is needed. (b) Describe a test to show that propene is unsaturated. (c) Suggest why hydrogen is also a useful product of some cracking reactions.
items.answer: (a) Demand for smaller alkanes (petrol) and alkenes is greater than the supply from fractional distillation; long chains are less useful. (b) Aqueous bromine turns from orange to colourless. (c) It can be used as a fuel or to make ammonia/margarine.

items.stem: What is seen when ethene is bubbled through aqueous bromine?
options: The solution turns from orange to colourless
The solution turns from colourless to orange
items.answer: The solution turns from orange to colourless

items.stem: Which type of reaction occurs when an alkene reacts with hydrogen?
items.answer: addition
items.markingKey: H₂ adds across the C=C bond (Ni catalyst) to form an alkane.

items.stem: Explain why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes.
items.answer: The C=C double bond can open up, allowing atoms to add across it.

items.stem: Explain why the addition of hydrogen to an alkene is important in the food industry.
items.answer: It converts unsaturated vegetable oils into saturated fats (margarine) with a higher melting point.

items.stem: But-1-ene reacts with bromine. Name the product, give its structural formula, write the equation using molecular formulae and state the conditions.
items.answer: 1,2-dibromobutane; CH₂BrCHBrCH₂CH₃; C₄H₈ + Br₂ → C₄H₈Br₂; room temperature; aqueous bromine (no catalyst)
items.markingKey: 1 mark product name/structure; 1 mark equation; 1 mark conditions [3]

items.stem: Calculate the mass of bromine that reacts exactly with 28.0 g of ethene, and the mass of product formed. C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂
items.answer: 160 g Br₂; 188 g product

items.stem: Propene reacts with bromine. Name the product, give its structural formula, write the equation using molecular formulae and state the conditions.
items.answer: 1,2-dibromopropane; CH₂BrCHBrCH₃; C₃H₆ + Br₂ → C₃H₆Br₂; room temperature; aqueous bromine (no catalyst)
items.markingKey: 1 mark product name/structure; 1 mark equation; 1 mark conditions [3]

items.stem: Tariq cracks paraffin oil in the laboratory by passing its vapour over heated broken pottery (a catalyst). (a) Write the balanced equation for cracking C₁₂H₂₆ into C₈H₁₈ and ethene. (b) Explain why cracking is needed. (c) Describe a test to show that ethene is unsaturated.
items.answer: (a) C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ + 2C₂H₄ (b) Demand for smaller alkanes (petrol) and alkenes is greater than the supply from fractional distillation; long chains are less useful. (c) Aqueous bromine turns from orange to colourless.

items.stem: What are the conditions for making ethanol by fermentation?
items.answer: yeast, 25–35 °C, absence of oxygen
items.markingKey: Glucose → ethanol + CO₂ using enzymes in yeast, anaerobic, warm.

items.stem: Explain why fermentation is carried out in the absence of air.
items.answer: With oxygen, yeast respires aerobically to CO₂ and water (and ethanol can be oxidised to ethanoic acid), so no ethanol is produced.

items.stem: Explain why fermentation stops when the ethanol concentration reaches about 15%.
items.answer: Ethanol becomes toxic to the yeast and kills it.

items.stem: Calculate the maximum mass of ethanol that can be made by fermenting 180 g of glucose. C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
Calculate the maximum mass of ethanol that can be made by fermenting 45 g of glucose. C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂

A biofuel plant in Toronto ferments sugar cane juice to make ethanol. (a) Calculate the mass of ethanol that could be made from 360 g of glucose. (b) Write the equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.
items.answer: (a) 184 g (b) C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O

items.stem: Explain why ethanol made by fermentation can be described as a renewable (biofuel).
items.answer: It is made from sugar from crops that can be regrown each year.

items.stem: Explain why ethanol from fermentation must be fractionally distilled.
items.answer: The mixture contains only about 15% ethanol in water and other substances; ethanol (b.p. 78 °C) is separated from water (b.p. 100 °C).

items.stem: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of methanol.
items.answer: 2CH₃OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 4H₂O

items.stem: Ethanol is used as a fuel. Write the balanced equation for its complete combustion and calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed when 23.0 g burns.
items.answer: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O; 44.0 g

items.stem: A biofuel plant in Istanbul ferments sugar cane juice to make ethanol. (a) State the conditions for fermentation. (b) Calculate the mass of ethanol that could be made from 900 g of glucose. (c) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of fermentation compared with the addition of steam to ethene.
items.answer: (a) Yeast; 25–35 °C; absence of oxygen (anaerobic); aqueous glucose. (b) 460 g (c) Advantage: renewable raw material / low temperature. Disadvantage: slow / batch process / impure product needing distillation.

items.stem: Why is ethanoic acid described as a weak acid?
options: It does not react with metals
It is only partially dissociated into ions in water
items.answer: It is only partially dissociated into ions in water
items.markingKey: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ — only a small fraction ionises.

items.stem: Explain why ethanoic acid reacts more slowly with magnesium than hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.
items.answer: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid — only partially dissociated — so the concentration of H⁺ ions is lower.

items.stem: Explain why a 0.1 mol/dm³ solution of ethanoic acid has a higher pH than 0.1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: Ethanoic acid is weak and only partly ionised, so [H⁺] is lower; HCl is fully ionised.

items.stem: Propanoic acid reacts with calcium carbonate. Describe what you would observe, name the products and write the balanced equation.
items.answer: Fizzing; the solid dissolves; calcium propanoate, water and carbon dioxide; 2CH₃CH₂COOH + CaCO₃ → (CH₃CH₂COO)₂Ca + H₂O + CO₂
items.markingKey: 1 mark observation; 1 mark products; 1 mark equation [3]

items.stem: Name the ester formed when propanoic acid reacts with ethanol, and state the conditions needed.
items.answer: ethyl propanoate; warm with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (catalyst).

items.stem: Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide. Describe what you would observe, name the products and write the balanced equation.
items.answer: No visible change (temperature rises); sodium ethanoate and water; CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O
items.markingKey: 1 mark observation; 1 mark products; 1 mark equation [3]

items.stem: Tomás investigates the reactions of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH. (a) Name the alcohol needed to make methyl ethanoate from ethanoic acid, and state the conditions. (b) Give the structural formula of methyl ethanoate. (c) Suggest a use of esters.
items.answer: (a) methanol; warm with concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst. (b) CH₃COOCH₃ (c) Flavourings, perfumes or solvents.

items.stem: A food-flavouring company makes the ester propyl propanoate from propanoic acid. (a) State the functional group in propanoic acid. (b) Describe what is seen when calcium carbonate is added and write the equation. (c) Suggest a use of esters.
items.answer: (a) –COOH (b) Fizzing; the solid dissolves; 2CH₃CH₂COOH + CaCO₃ → (CH₃CH₂COO)₂Ca + H₂O + CO₂ (c) Flavourings, perfumes or solvents.

items.stem: What is the catalyst for esterification?
items.answer: concentrated sulfuric acid
items.markingKey: Acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water with a few drops of conc. H₂SO₄, warmed.

items.stem: Explain why wine left open to the air turns sour.
items.answer: Bacteria oxidise the ethanol to ethanoic acid (vinegar) using oxygen from the air.

items.stem: Explain why esterification is described as a condensation reaction.
items.answer: Two molecules join together and a small molecule (water) is eliminated.

items.stem: Freya compares 1.0 mol/dm³ propanoic acid with 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid by measuring their electrical conductivity. Predict the result and explain it.
items.answer: The carboxylic acid conducts less well: propanoic acid is a weak acid, only partially dissociated, so fewer ions in solution; hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, fully dissociated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark weak = partially dissociated; 1 mark link to H⁺/ions [3]

items.stem: Name the ester formed when ethanoic acid reacts with propan-1-ol, and state the conditions needed.
items.answer: propyl ethanoate; warm with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (catalyst).

items.stem: Excess sodium carbonate is added to 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid. 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed at r.t.p., in cm³.
items.answer: 600 cm³

items.stem: Aisha investigates the reactions of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH. (a) Name the alcohol needed to make methyl ethanoate from ethanoic acid, and state the conditions. (b) Describe how ethanoic acid can be made from ethanol.
items.answer: (a) methanol; warm with concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst. (b) Oxidation with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII), or by bacterial oxidation in air.

items.stem: Vinegar sold in Colombo contains ethanoic acid. A student studies methanoic acid, a member of the same homologous series. (a) State the functional group in methanoic acid. (b) Describe what is seen when calcium carbonate is added and write the equation. (c) Give the structural formula of propyl methanoate. (d) Suggest a use of esters.
items.answer: (a) –COOH (b) Fizzing; the solid dissolves; 2HCOOH + CaCO₃ → (HCOO)₂Ca + H₂O + CO₂ (c) HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃ (d) Flavourings, perfumes or solvents.

items.stem: What type of reaction occurs between ethane and chlorine in UV light?
items.answer: substitution
items.markingKey: A hydrogen atom is replaced by a chlorine atom.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why incomplete combustion of alkanes is dangerous in homes. (b) Explain why a mixture of products forms when methane reacts with excess chlorine.
items.answer: (a) With too little oxygen, carbon monoxide forms; it is colourless, odourless and toxic. (b) More than one hydrogen can be substituted in turn: CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄ can all form.

items.stem: Methane reacts with chlorine in the presence of ultraviolet light. Name the organic product, write the equation and state the type of reaction.
items.answer: chloromethane; CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl; substitution (photochemical)
items.markingKey: 1 mark name; 1 mark equation; 1 mark substitution [3]

items.stem: Ravi investigates the reactions of propane, a member of the alkane homologous series. (a) Write the balanced equation for complete combustion. (b) Name the toxic gas formed if the supply of air is limited, and explain why it is toxic.
items.answer: (a) C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O (b) Carbon monoxide: it reduces the ability of the blood to carry oxygen.

items.stem: Why is cracking important to oil refineries?
options: It removes sulfur from crude oil
It converts large, less useful alkanes into smaller, more useful alkanes and alkenes
items.answer: It converts large, less useful alkanes into smaller, more useful alkanes and alkenes
items.markingKey: Demand for petrol and alkenes exceeds supply from distillation.

items.stem: Two unlabelled gas jars contain pentane and but-1-ene. Describe a chemical test that would show which jar contains but-1-ene, giving the result for each gas and explaining the difference.
items.answer: Shake each with aqueous bromine. But-1-ene: orange → colourless (addition across C=C). Pentane: stays orange (saturated, no addition).
items.markingKey: 1 mark reagent; 1 mark each result; 1 mark explanation [4]

items.stem: Two unlabelled gas jars contain butane and propene. Describe a chemical test that would show which jar contains propene, giving the result for each gas and explaining the difference.
items.answer: Shake each with aqueous bromine. Propene: orange → colourless (addition across C=C). Butane: stays orange (saturated, no addition).
items.markingKey: 1 mark reagent; 1 mark each result; 1 mark explanation [4]

items.stem: Complete and balance the equation for the cracking of C₈H₁₈ into C₆H₁₄ and ethene only: C₈H₁₈ → C₆H₁₄ + ...
items.answer: C₈H₁₈ → C₆H₁₄ + C₂H₄

items.stem: Calculate the mass of bromine that reacts exactly with 2.10 g of ethene, and the mass of product formed. C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂
items.answer: 12.0 g Br₂; 14.1 g product

items.stem: Aisha cracks paraffin oil in the laboratory by passing its vapour over heated broken pottery (a catalyst). (a) State the conditions needed for cracking. (b) Write the balanced equation for cracking C₁₂H₂₆ into C₆H₁₄ and ethene. (c) Suggest why hydrogen is also a useful product of some cracking reactions.
items.answer: (a) High temperature (about 500 °C) and a catalyst (e.g. aluminium oxide/silica). (b) C₁₂H₂₆ → C₆H₁₄ + 3C₂H₄ (c) It can be used as a fuel or to make ammonia/margarine.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Give a use of ethanol. (b) Why is the temperature in fermentation kept below about 40 °C?
items.answer: (a) As a fuel or as a solvent (b) Higher temperatures denature the enzymes in yeast
items.markingKey: (a) Ethanol burns cleanly and dissolves many substances. (b) Enzymes are proteins that lose their shape when too hot.

items.stem: A company in Singapore must decide whether to make ethanol by fermentation or by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene. Compare the two methods in terms of temperature and energy use.
items.answer: Temperature: fermentation 25–35 °C, hydration about 300 °C. Energy use: fermentation low, hydration high (high temperature and pressure).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each correct comparison for each factor (both methods) [4]

items.stem: Ethanol is manufactured by the addition of steam to ethene: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH. Calculate the mass of ethanol formed from 2.80 tonnes of ethene, and state the conditions used.
items.answer: 4.60 tonnes; phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300 °C, 6000 kPa
items.markingKey: 28 t ethene → 46 t ethanol [1]; mass = 4.60 t [1]; conditions [1]

items.stem: Mateo sets up a fermentation experiment using glucose solution and yeast in a conical flask fitted with an airlock. (a) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of fermentation compared with the addition of steam to ethene. (b) Write the equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.
items.answer: (a) Advantage: renewable raw material / low temperature. Disadvantage: slow / batch process / impure product needing distillation. (b) C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O

items.stem: Priya compares 0.50 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid with 0.50 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid by measuring their rate of reaction with magnesium ribbon. Predict the result and explain it.
items.answer: The carboxylic acid fizzes more slowly: ethanoic acid is a weak acid, only partially dissociated, so lower [H⁺]; hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, fully dissociated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark weak = partially dissociated; 1 mark link to H⁺/ions [3]

items.stem: Ethan compares 0.50 mol/dm³ methanoic acid with 0.50 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid by measuring their pH. Predict the result and explain it.
items.answer: The ethanoic-type acid has the higher pH (about 3 vs 1): methanoic acid is a weak acid, only partially dissociated, so lower [H⁺]; hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, fully dissociated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark weak = partially dissociated; 1 mark link to H⁺/ions [3]

items.stem: Excess calcium carbonate is added to 25.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid. 2CH₃COOH + CaCO₃ → (CH₃COO)₂Ca + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed at r.t.p., in cm³.
items.answer: 150 cm³

items.stem: Name the ester formed when methanoic acid reacts with propan-1-ol, and state the conditions needed.
items.answer: propyl methanoate; warm with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (catalyst).

items.stem: Vinegar sold in Nairobi contains ethanoic acid. A student studies propanoic acid, a member of the same homologous series. (a) Explain why propanoic acid is described as a weak acid. (b) Give the structural formula of methyl propanoate.
items.answer: (a) It is only partially dissociated into H⁺ ions in aqueous solution. (b) CH₃CH₂COOCH₃

items.stem: Ravi investigates the reactions of methanoic acid, HCOOH. (a) State the functional group in methanoic acid. (b) Describe what is seen when calcium carbonate is added and write the equation. (c) Give the structural formula of methyl methanoate. (d) Suggest a use of esters.
items.answer: (a) –COOH (b) Fizzing; the solid dissolves; 2HCOOH + CaCO₃ → (HCOO)₂Ca + H₂O + CO₂ (c) HCOOCH₃ (d) Flavourings, perfumes or solvents.

items.stem: Why are alkanes described as generally unreactive?
options: They contain only strong C–C and C–H single bonds
items.answer: They contain only strong C–C and C–H single bonds
items.markingKey: Alkanes are saturated; apart from combustion and substitution they react little.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why alkanes are used as fuels. (b) Explain why a mixture of products forms when methane reacts with excess chlorine.
items.answer: (a) Their combustion is very exothermic, releasing a lot of energy, and they burn cleanly in excess oxygen. (b) More than one hydrogen can be substituted in turn: CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄ can all form.

items.stem: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide and the mass of water formed when 60.0 g of propane burns completely. C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
items.answer: 180 g CO₂; 98.2 g H₂O

items.stem: Samuel investigates the reactions of butane, a member of the alkane homologous series. (a) Calculate the volume of oxygen needed to burn 100 cm³ of butane completely. (b) Describe the reaction of butane with chlorine, including the conditions and the type of reaction.
items.answer: (a) 650 cm³ (b) UV light; substitution — an H atom is replaced by Cl, forming a chloroalkane and HCl.

items.stem: Which product of cracking could be used to make polymers?
items.answer: ethene
items.markingKey: Alkenes are monomers for addition polymers.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes. (b) Explain why cracking always produces at least one unsaturated product.
items.answer: (a) The C=C double bond can open up, allowing atoms to add across it. (b) A long alkane does not have enough hydrogen atoms for all the smaller molecules to be saturated, so at least one alkene (or H₂) forms.

items.stem: Two unlabelled gas jars contain propane and propene. Describe a chemical test that would show which jar contains propene, giving the result for each gas and explaining the difference.
items.answer: Shake each with aqueous bromine. Propene: orange → colourless (addition across C=C). Propane: stays orange (saturated, no addition).
items.markingKey: 1 mark reagent; 1 mark each result; 1 mark explanation [4]

items.stem: Complete and balance the equation for the cracking of C₁₆H₃₄ into C₁₀H₂₂ and ethene only: C₁₆H₃₄ → C₁₀H₂₂ + ...
items.answer: C₁₆H₃₄ → C₁₀H₂₂ + 3C₂H₄

(b) Name the product formed when ethene reacts with steam, and give the conditions. (c) Suggest why hydrogen is also a useful product of some cracking reactions.
items.answer: (a) Demand for smaller alkanes (petrol) and alkenes is greater than the supply from fractional distillation; long chains are less useful. (b) ethanol; phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300 °C and 6000 kPa (60 atm) (c) It can be used as a fuel or to make ammonia/margarine.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which equation represents fermentation? (b) What is the catalyst for the addition of steam to ethene?
items.answer: (a) C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ (b) phosphoric acid
items.markingKey: (a) Glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide. (b) C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, H₃PO₄ catalyst, 300 °C, 6000 kPa.

items.stem: A company in Mexico City must decide whether to make ethanol by fermentation or by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene. Compare the two methods in terms of energy use and raw material.
items.answer: Energy use: fermentation low, hydration high (high temperature and pressure). Raw material: fermentation renewable (sugars from crops), hydration non-renewable (ethene from petroleum).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each correct comparison for each factor (both methods) [4]

items.answer: (a) 92.0 g (b) Advantage: renewable raw material / low temperature. Disadvantage: slow / batch process / impure product needing distillation.

items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark weak = partially dissociated; 1 mark link to H⁺/ions [3]

items.answer: The carboxylic acid fizzes more slowly: propanoic acid is a weak acid, only partially dissociated, so lower [H⁺]; hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, fully dissociated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark weak = partially dissociated; 1 mark link to H⁺/ions [3]

items.stem: Excess sodium carbonate is added to 40.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ propanoic acid. 2CH₃CH₂COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃CH₂COONa + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed at r.t.p., in cm³.
items.answer: 240 cm³

items.stem: Name the ester formed when methanoic acid reacts with ethanol, and state the conditions needed.
items.answer: ethyl methanoate; warm with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (catalyst).

items.stem: Excess sodium carbonate is added to 40.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid. 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed at r.t.p., in cm³.
items.answer: 480 cm³

items.stem: Vinegar sold in Mumbai contains ethanoic acid. A student studies propanoic acid, a member of the same homologous series. (a) Describe what is seen when potassium hydroxide is added and write the equation. (b) Suggest a use of esters. (c) Describe how ethanoic acid can be made from ethanol.
items.answer: (a) No visible change (temperature rises); CH₃CH₂COOH + KOH → CH₃CH₂COOK + H₂O (b) Flavourings, perfumes or solvents. (c) Oxidation with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII), or by bacterial oxidation in air.
